primary_secondary.note: Replication study generating new lab data.

study_type.claude: Experiment (external close replication of a controlled lab experiment)
study_type.note: External close replication of the Züger and Fritz (2015) lab study.

research_method.claude: External close replication (Group I) of a controlled lab experiment with biometric sensors; ML classification (Naïve Bayes, Weka) with 10×10-fold CV vs. majority classifier; short post-interviews; 82 interruption samples, ~10 h of biophysical data
research_method.nlm: External close replication, quantitative; Naïve Bayes via Weka, WrapperSubsetEval feature selection, 10x10-fold cross-validation; 82 interruption samples over 10 hours of programming sessions
research_method.value: External close replication of a controlled lab experiment (Züger and Fritz 2015); 10 one-on-one 60-minute programming sessions with tablet interruptions, 82 interruption samples, ~10 hours of biometric data (EEG, ECG, EDA, skin temperature); Naïve Bayes classification (Weka, wrapper-based feature selection) evaluated by 10×10-fold CV against a majority-class baseline; post-session interview/questionnaire

context.claude: Academic; university lab (Vienna University of Economics and Business), code-change tasks on JHotDraw; 10 participants (4 graduate, 2 undergraduate, 3 professionals, 1 HTL graduate)
context.nlm: Academic/laboratory setting (Vienna University of Economics and Business), JHotDraw Java maintenance tasks; 10 participants (same breakdown)
context.value: academic; controlled university lab (Vienna University of Economics and Business), three code-change tasks on the Java code base of JHotDraw; 10 participants (4 graduate students, 2 undergraduate students, 3 professionals, 1 HTL graduate)

ai_discussed.note: ML (Naïve Bayes) is the instrument evaluated for automatically measuring developer interruptibility; no AI coding tools.

remote_covid.note: On-site lab study. Full text has one speculative sentence on post-COVID work environment (notifications vs. in-person interruptions, p. 22).

data_window.note: Not stated by either (only submission/publication dates).

cat_productivity.note: NotebookLM labels interruption/resumption/edit lag as Productivity; Claude labels the lags Activity/Flow. Paper uses lags as indicators of interruptibility; perceived productivity only as motivation.

cat_quality.note: NotebookLM labels self-reported task completion/difficulty as Quality, which is not a quality metric under the definition.

cat_satisfaction.note: Borderline: perceived disturbance and mental workload ratings (both extractors label them generic DevEx); no satisfaction/well-being measure.

cat_activity.note: Both use the label Activity for lags (Claude) or biometric signals (NotebookLM); no repository activity metrics.

cat_devex.note: DevEx framework not used (Claude: not reported); 'DevEx' labels on metrics are generic.

cat_survey.note: Five-point Likert self-reports of interruptibility (target variable), mental workload and disturbance; post-session questionnaire.

evidence.quote: We conducted an external close replication of the original lab study. As such, we held ten one-on-one sessions in which participants were asked to perform three code change tasks during a 60-minute programming session

Biophysical data on brain, eye, heart, and skin activity were collected from ten participants for a total of ten hours. Using a Naïve Bayes classifier, we were not able to generate models that performed significantly better than the proposed baseline (majority classifier).
model performance is measured in terms of the average accuracy which the model configuration scores in the 10x10-fold cross-validation (CV) step
All participants in the lab study had to work on the following three code-change tasks in the Java code base of JHotDraw
They had a diverse academic profile with four graduate students, two undergraduate students, three professionals, and one HTL13 graduate.
evidence.loc: PDF p. 11 ("13" is a footnote marker)

evidence.quote: Can biometric sensors be used to automatically measure interruptibility of software developers with high accuracy in a controlled (lab) environment?

The participants' ratings of perceived interruptibility were collected on a five-point Likert scale : 1 ("very interruptible")-5 ("very uninterruptible"). This also applies to perceived disturbance of the interruption and the mental load at the time of the interruption.
